newsitem.title: USA: Orange County's former treasurer awaits sentencing.
newsitem.headline: Orange County's former treasurer awaits sentencing.

text.p: Former Orange County, Calif., Treasurer Robert Citron, whose ill-advised investments led to the county's bankruptcy, awaited sentencing Monday for crimes related to the unprecedented financial crisis.

Superior Court Judge J. Stephen Czuleger was expected to hear testimony here Monday and possibly Tuesday from those hurt by the county's bankruptcy and from Citron's supporters before handing the ex-treasurer his long-awaited sentence.

Citron, widely blamed for the county's financial crisis, pleaded guilty in April 1995 to six felonies, including counts of making untrue statements in the sale of securities and misappropriating public funds.
Citron, who has been cooperating with prosecutors, faces up to 14 years in prison.

The county filed for bankruptcy protection Dec. 6, 1994, after sustaining losses of more than $1.6 billion on risky investments. It was the largest municipal bankruptcy in U.S. history. The county emerged from bankruptcy last June.
In court papers filed earlier this month, Orange County District Attorney Michael Capizzi recommended that Citron be sentenced to seven years in prison and a $400,000 fine.
"Since his plea, defendant (Citron) has been candid, truthful and accommodating -- as he agreed to be at the time he pleaded guilty," the district attorney said.
The district attorney added, however, that Citron's "crimes and the financial damage caused by him are too serious" to justify granting him probation.
Citron attorney David Wiechert called the district attorney's sentencing recommendation "incredibly harsh."
Wiechert said Citron, 71, had already "paid dearly" for his crimes.

"The privacy and intimacy he once shared with his wife in their modest home has been shattered by glaring TV cameras and trash-scrounging reporters," he said. "A prison term would take away the last vestiges of Mr. Citron's reason for being."
Wiechert has painted a tragic portrait of Citron.

Court documents contended that Citron suffers from dementia and other brain dysfunctions resulting in memory loss and other problems. Wiechert said Citron's "mental limitations caught up with him" and that his psychological "deficits" rendered him susceptible to the advice of trusted counsellors, such as investment giant Merrill Lynch & Co.
Wiechert recently released psychological evaluations indicating that Citron was "seriously impaired" in executive functioning, a key part of his job as county treasurer.
Merrill Lynch maintains that Citron was an experienced and sophisticated treasurer who made his own investment decisions.
Wiechert said Citron should receive probation and a fine of $10,000. If any confinement were to be required, his client should only receive home detention, the attorney said.
